title: Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive: FAQ for market participants
issuing_body: European Union (Directive) / Fact sheet prepared by Bloomberg
document_type: FAQ / fact sheet summarising EU Directive requirements
scope: Large EU companies, listed SMEs and certain non-EU companies with significant EU activity
overall_summary: Explains who is in scope of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, when reporting starts, what must be reported using the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, and how this information will be made available to the market.

structure.title: What is the CSRD?
structure.summary: Introduces the CSRD as the EU’s updated framework for mandatory sustainability reporting, replacing and expanding the Non-Financial Reporting Directive.
key_points: The Directive entered into force in January 2023 and the first set of European Sustainability Reporting Standards was adopted in July 2023.
It modernises and strengthens disclosure rules on environmental, social and governance information that companies must report.
Companies subject to CSRD must report using ESRS developed by EFRAG, an independent technical advisory body.
The aim is to improve the quality, comparability and reliability of sustainability information available to investors and other stakeholders.

structure.title: Regulatory and reporting timeline
structure.summary: Shows the phased introduction of CSRD requirements and ESRS standards, and when different categories of companies start reporting.
key_points: On 5 January 2023, the Directive entered into force.
On 31 July 2023, the first set of sector-agnostic ESRS was published.
Further standards are planned: SME standards, sector-specific standards and third-country standards, with consultations scheduled between 2023 and 2024.
Companies previously covered by the NFRD report under CSRD for financial year 2024.
Large companies that were not under NFRD start reporting on financial year 2025.
Listed SMEs report on financial year 2026, with an option to defer until 2028.
Certain non-EU companies with substantial EU turnover and presence are expected to report for financial year 2028.

structure.title: Which companies are in scope?
structure.summary: Describes the categories of companies required to report under CSRD, including EU and non-EU entities.
key_points: Covers large EU companies that meet size thresholds in terms of turnover, balance sheet total and number of employees.
Applies to EU-listed companies, including listed SMEs, with some phase-in and opt-out possibilities.
Includes specific criteria for non-EU companies with significant EU turnover and either a large EU subsidiary or a substantial EU branch.
Aligns sustainability reporting obligations with the importance of the company’s activities and footprint in the EU market.

structure.title: European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS)
structure.summary: Summarises the ESRS architecture and the main topical standards companies must use when preparing CSRD reports.
key_points: ESRS 1 sets general requirements for sustainability reporting and ESRS 2 defines general disclosures that all in-scope companies must provide.
Topical standards are grouped into environmental, social and governance categories.
Environmental standards include: E1 Climate Change, E2 Pollution, E3 Water and Marine Resources, E4 Biodiversity and Ecosystems, E5 Circular Economy.
Social standards cover: S1 Own Workforce, S2 Workers in the Value Chain, S3 Affected Communities, S4 Consumers and End-users.
Governance is addressed through G1 Business Conduct.
Together these standards define over 500 data points that must be considered in the materiality assessment and reported if material.

structure.title: Key features of CSRD reporting
structure.summary: Highlights the main conceptual and practical innovations in CSRD compared to previous EU non-financial reporting rules.
key_points: Double materiality: companies must assess both their impacts on people and the environment and how sustainability matters affect the company’s financial performance and prospects.
Targets: companies are required to disclose targets, including absolute greenhouse gas reduction targets for at least 2030 and 2050, as well as baselines and progress.
Assurance: limited assurance over sustainability disclosures is mandatory from the start, carried out by an independent auditor or assurance provider.
Value chain coverage: reporting is extended beyond the company’s own operations to relevant parts of its upstream and downstream value chain, including outside the EU where applicable.
Standardisation: common ESRS-based templates improve comparability of sustainability data across companies and sectors.
Digital accessibility: sustainability statements will ultimately be digitally tagged and made available through an EU-wide access point, enhancing usability for data users.

structure.title: What data will be disclosed and how can it be used?
structure.summary: Explains the types of information expected in CSRD reports and how market participants can use the data.
key_points: Data covers environmental topics such as greenhouse gas emissions, energy use, water, pollution, biodiversity and circular economy metrics.
Social disclosures address workforce conditions, human rights, diversity and inclusion, communities and consumer impacts.
Governance disclosures include business conduct, anti-corruption, risk management and oversight structures.
Information is structured to support investors’ and lenders’ needs, including SFDR and EU Taxonomy-related disclosures.
CSRD data will be accessible via public filings and platforms that aggregate and standardise ESG data.

structure.title: Implications for in-scope companies
structure.summary: Outlines the practical consequences of CSRD for corporate strategy, data systems and governance.
key_points: Companies need to build or upgrade sustainability data collection systems, including controls and audit trails.
Boards and senior management must integrate sustainability considerations into strategy, risk management and oversight.
Engagement with suppliers and other value chain partners is required to collect necessary information and manage impacts.
Internal capacity-building is needed to perform robust double materiality assessments and interpret ESRS requirements.
Increased transparency can affect access to capital, cost of financing and stakeholder expectations.

structure.title: Implications for investors and other market participants
structure.summary: Describes how CSRD data can be used by investors, lenders, rating agencies and other stakeholders.
key_points: Provides more standardised, comparable and reliable ESG information across a much larger universe of companies than under the previous directive.
Supports regulatory reporting needs under SFDR, the EU Taxonomy and other sustainable finance regulations.
Enables better integration of sustainability factors into credit analysis, equity research and risk models.
Helps identify leaders and laggards on sustainability performance and transition readiness.
Supports engagement and stewardship activities based on more granular and assured disclosures.
